title: Zombie Outbreak: 30 Days Trapped On The 30th Floor

segments.text: You live on the 30th floor.
Until tonight, that was the worst thing about your flat.
At 9.40, every phone in the building screams at once.
Stay inside, lock your doors, do not help the injured.
30 floors down, the street is full of people running.
Some of them are not running away.
Your neighbor is in the hallway, knocking on every door.
His arm is bandaged.
You watch through the peephole and you do not open.
First problem, water.
A tower pumps it up with electricity.
When the power dies, the top floors go dry first.
So you fill the bathtub, about 40 gallons.
Then every pot, every bottle, the sink,
one person needs a gallon a day.
You have just bought yourself six weeks.
By morning, the sirens have stopped.
That is worse.
You count the food.
11 days if you eat normally, 25 if you don't.
So you ration.
From now on, everything is a number.
Eat the fridge first, then the freezer, cans last.
Once the power goes, a closed freezer stays cold
for about two days.
The neighbor is still in the hallway.
He is standing very straight now.
He has been facing your door since three in the morning.
The power dies at noon.
The taps cough and stop.
You were right about the water.
Second problem, the stairs.
The lifts are dead, so nothing rides up.
But they can climb.
They are just slow.
You push the couch against the door, then the bookshelf.
Then you sit very still and you listen.
First rule of a siege, noise is a dinner bell.
No music, no shouting, shoes off.
From up here, you can see the whole city.
Three fires, no fire engines.
Third problem, one of those fires
is in your building, floor 11.
Smoke climbs faster than anything dead.
You cannot go down.
So you soak towels and seal the gaps around the door.
In a tower fire, smoke kills more people than flames.
By night, it burns itself out against the concrete.
It cost you four gallons you could not spare.
It rains.
You put every bowl you own on the window ledge.
You win back three gallons.
Across the street, on the roof of the bank,
someone has painted a message in white.
You need binoculars to read it.
It says, count them.
So you go to the peephole and you count.
Yesterday, there were four in the hallway.
Today, there are nine.
They are not wandering.
Every one of them is facing your door.
And behind you, from inside the flat,
something knocks twice on the bathroom wall.
You stand in the bathroom doorway holding a frying pan.
The knocking comes again.
Two, then three.
It is not coming from the bath.
It is coming from the pipes.
Behind the wall panel is the service shaft.
Every flat on this side shares it.
Someone next door is tapping on it.
You tap back with a spoon.
Three, a pause.
Then, from the other side, three.
For the first time in 10 days, you are not alone.
New problem, and nobody warns you about this one.
The toilet stopped flushing on day three.
So, a bucket, a bag, a lid.
And it stays far away from the bathtub.
In long sieges, dirty water has killed more people
than the fighting.
33 gallons, 14 days of food.
You open the window.
Three meters away, she opens hers.
Red glasses.
She has not spoken to anyone in 13 days either.
You cannot reach each other.
So, you build a ferry, a rope, a bucket, and a coat hanger.
She is down to her last two gallons.
You send a full jug across.
She sends back the one thing you do not have,
a radio and a bag of batteries, two people.
From today, everything runs out twice as fast.
You are sick of cold beans.
And there is a camping stove in the cupboard.
Do not light it.
You sealed this flat against smoke.
A flame in a sealed room makes carbon monoxide,
and you would never smell it coming.
Cold beans it is, half a tin each.
At night, the radio finds a voice.
Survivors are gathering at the stadium.
Come on foot, bring nothing.
She wants to go.
You think about the hallway.
On the bank roof, there is a second message.
Shorter this time.
It says, roof.
You answer with a shaving mirror.
On a clear day, a flash of sunlight carries for miles.
Three flashes.
You wait.
The figure on the roof flashes back, twice.
You stop counting at 23.
They do not leave.
They do not sleep.
They leave.
At night, the door begins to creak.
A door does not break in the middle.
It breaks at the latch and the frame.
So that is where you brace it.
A bed plank, wedged at 45 degrees
between the door frame and the floor.
It buys you days, not weeks.
15 gallons.
Eight days of food, if you can call half a tin a day food.
But a tower like this keeps water on the roof.
A tank, thousands of gallons for the fire system.
The roof is four floors up.
The stairs are full.
That leaves the shaft.
Pipes, dust and an iron rung every half meter.
The same shaft she knocked on.
It goes all the way up.
First, the hallway.
Rule one said noise is a dinner bell.
Time to ring it.
You wind the alarm, set it for two minutes
and drop it down the rubbish chute.
30 floors down, it starts to ring.
In the hallway, every head turns.
23 becomes four.
You both climb.
Four floors.
Three points of contact, always.
Two hands in a foot or two feet in a hand.
At the top, there is a hatch.
It is not locked.
Sky, wind and a steel tank the size of a bus.
The gauge says half full, 5,000 gallons.
Water is solved, food is not.
You paint your own message on the roof
in strokes three meters tall.
From up here, you can finally see the bank roof properly.
The figure waves with both arms.
Then points again and again at its own ear.
You do not understand, not yet.
The first night outside nearly ends you both.
Up here, the wind strips the heat out of you
faster than cold alone ever could.
So you build low.
A windbreak event covers and a tarpolin
on the sheltered side of the tank
and cardboard underneath.
The ground steals more heat than the air does.
You sleep four hours.
It feels like a holiday.
The bank roof is empty.
The paint tin is lying on its side.
The last message is not finished.
Three words, do not trust.
The radio says the stadium is safe.
It says so every hour in the same voice
with the same pause in the same place.
She wants to go.
You want to know how that sentence ends.
Pigeons roost on the tank every evening.
You look at them.
She looks at you.
You are not there yet.
Half a tin a day each is about 200 calories.
A body needs 10 times that.
In a week, you will be too weak to climb.
On the 30th night, the door finally goes.
They pour into a flat with nobody in it.
You hear it from four floors up,
sitting on the hatch with everything heavy you could find.
Two days of food, a city of them below.
And on the bank roof, a light comes on.
Someone has finished the message.
Do not trust the radio.
She is already holding it
and it has started talking again.
